name: San peoples
subtitle: San peoples: who the sources name, where they live, and what the old labels got wrong.

keyPoints.text: About 113,000 people (2016): Approximate total of San in six southern African countries (Angola, Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe), compiled by the report authors from San organisations (WIMSA, national councils, etc.) and governments.

Terminology: 'San' is the generic term adopted by San organisations (WIMSA 2003) and widely used by anthropologists; in Botswana the official term is Basarwa; 'Bushmen' is also widely used. The author argues the context of use and the wishes of the people named should guide the choice, rather than etymology. Use of group names is increasing.

The same overview says the term 'Khoesan' was rejected by WIMSA as a collective label (the volume's wording on this is in the same chapter; the quote below is on the Botswana official term and the neutral-term 'Remote Area Dweller' being resented).

parts.text: The same overview says the term 'Khoesan' was rejected by WIMSA as a collective label (the volume's wording on this is in the same chapter; the quote below is on the Botswana official term and the neutral-term 'Remote Area Dweller' being resented).
Group names: no single self-designation is shared by all; in Zimbabwe, San generally identify as Tshwa, and the Ndebele terms Amasili or Abatwa are used by others.
An academic historian avoids 'Bushmen' because of its derogatory tone (except in quotations) and uses 'San' for the Cape's hunter-gatherers.

Languages: the click languages of southern Africa are grouped into three families, Kx'a, Tuu and Khoe-Kwadi (older literature, such as the 2004 IWGIA volume, calls them Ju, Taa-!Ui and Khoe and groups them as 'Khoe-San'). Languages of all three families are in contact in the Central Kalahari.
Click consonants: the languages share clicks that are cross-linguistically rare and also attested in Hadza and Sandawe of Tanzania (a linguistic source).

Language families differ from each other as much as Indo-European from Finno-Ugric; individual languages named include Ju|'hoan, Naro, !Xoo, Khwe and N|u (several with only a few thousand speakers, per 2004 estimates).
The EBSCO entry on San languages describes clicks as the most distinguishing feature and lists countries where they are spoken.
Adhikari describes the main agents of destruction of Cape San society as Dutch-speaking pastoralists and says the weak colonial state sanctioned violence (his argument, 2010).
McDonald notes that in the early 1800s Cape settlers widely expected San extinction, while stating that settler colonialism is not always genocidal (nuance in the scholarly debate).
Namibia: under South African administration from 1920, vagrancy laws particularly affected San (SAHO timeline).
EBSCO: San were denied land rights by successive precolonial African, colonial and postcolonial powers.
Some San groups, such as the Ju|'hoansi of north-western Botswana and north-eastern Namibia, overlap national borders; the IWGIA volume says this puts them in a special position vis-a-vis states.
Zimbabwe-Botswana: Tshwa have relatives on both sides of the border; some who crossed were arrested and deported (as reported by Tshwa to the researchers, 2016).

blocks.q: Myth or fact: San are 'living representatives' of how all humanity lived at the dawn of history.
blocks.explain: Saugestad calls this a myth and notes it coexists with opposite stereotypes (brutal savages, harmless people); she observes that such debates do little to benefit the average San person. The IWGIA 2016 report adds that the San are not one people but many groups, each with its own name, history and language.

items.when: c. 27,000 years ago (debris dates; disputed for the art itself)
items.text: Painted stone fragments at Apollo 11 rock shelter, Huns Mountains, Namibia, excavated 1969, are among the earliest known art in Africa. EBSCO notes the date refers to debris around the fragments, not necessarily the paintings.

Direct radiocarbon dating placed painting on rockshelter walls in south-eastern Botswana at 5723-4420 cal BP, reported as the earliest directly dated rock paintings in southern Africa (Bonneau et al., 2017).

Historian Mohamed Adhikari argues that San society in the Cape Colony was almost completely destroyed in the 18th and 19th centuries by land confiscation, massacre, forced labour and cultural suppression, and analyses the 1700-1795 Dutch East India Company period as genocide. This is the author's thesis; the debate is scholarly.
Historian Jared McDonald writes that commandos, both official and unofficial, killed thousands of San in the late eighteenth century.

Saugestad writes that German colonial administration ranked people in a racial hierarchy, and that settler press headlines in 1911 used the phrases 'Bushman Plague' and 'Bushman Danger' (citing Gordon 1992). South African Administration vagrancy laws from 1920 particularly affected San, per SAHO.

The Reserve was created in 1963 under British colonial rule, partly to protect residents who wanted to keep hunting and gathering. The Botswana government began asking residents to move in 1986, brought trucks to remove residents in 1997, and cut all services in 2002. The government said it was not 'forcing' residents to leave (Michael Taylor's account).

Botswana High Court (Sesana and Others v Attorney General, Misca. No. 52 of 2002), three judges with separate judgments: unanimously found the applicants were in possession of the land before 31 January 2002 and that refusing special game licences was unlawful; held the 2002 termination of services was not unlawful or unconstitutional (Dow J dissenting). Case record summary; the full judgment was not read.

Botswana Court of Appeal (Mosetlhanyane and others v Attorney General) built on the 2006 decision and held that, as lawful occupiers, the applicants had a right of access to water on the reserve; ESCR-Net summary.
